drafts.walkScript: Start at lines 23 and 24, where the Mole knocks over a rabbit. He then goes along 'chaffing the other rabbits', which means teasing them. On line 25 the rabbits look out 'to see what the row was about'. So the row is the noise and fuss the Mole had made. The rabbits are not quarrelling with each other, and nobody rows a boat.

Read line 49, which describes the face the Mole sees. The face is grave, yet it has 'the same twinkle in its eye'. A twinkle is a bright, lively look, so the face is not sad or upset. So grave here means serious and calm, with no unhappiness in it. 'Round' is a separate word for its shape, and nobody is buried here.

Line 21 says the party 'entered' the room. Lines 21 and 22 say it 'consisted of only five'. These five are Mr Bingley and the people who came with him. So a party here is a group of people who arrive together. It is not everyone at the assembly, and it is not the ball.

Line 24 gives Mr Bingley 'a pleasant countenance'. Line 25 adds his 'manners', so countenance and manners are two different things. On line 34 Mr Darcy has 'a most forbidding, disagreeable countenance'. Line 30 says he 'was looked at', so a countenance is something people see. So it means a person's face, and the look on it.

Line 6 names 'the tense rigidity' that Matthew would have seen. Rigidity means being stiff, so this is how her body was set. Line 7 says this stiffness belongs to 'her attitude and expression'. So attitude here is the way she was holding herself. Nothing in these lines calls her shy or awkward.

On lines 14 and 15 the girl prefers to stay outside the waiting room. Her reason, on lines 15 and 16, is 'more scope for imagination'. Imagination is the mind at work, and outside gave it more space. So scope means room for the mind to work. She says nothing about cool air or quiet, and no tool is shown.

Line 14 says 'of course I had a good bait' when they reached town. Calling it good shows it was something Beauty was glad to have. Line 15 adds that the master's business took 'a long time'. So Beauty had a long stop, and a good bait is a feed and a rest. A horse would not call a wait with nothing to eat good.

Line 48 gives two reasons the door was mistaken: 'the agitation and half darkness'. Line 4 shows that the night before was their first in 'the new house'. On a first night in a strange house, the family was worried and rushed about. Mother only finds the room next morning, on line 46, so finding it came later. So agitation here is the worried, rushed state of that night.

Read line 29 and find the words 'growing out of the top'. Something growing out of the top of a wall is a plant. Line 30 adds 'the window-shape' as a second, separate thing. So the elder is the growing one, a small tree or bush. An older member of a family cannot grow out of a wall.

Read line 45 and find the words 'being useful, or at least officious'. The words 'or at least' set officious just below being truly useful. So officious means trying to be useful but pushing a little too far. Line 45 says the speaker 'drew near', but that is what was done. It has nothing to do with holding an office.

Read line 4 and find what the wood-pigeon is 'brooding over'. It is brooding over 'its own sweet voice', which is its call. A bird cannot sit on a sound to hatch it, so eggs do not fit. So brooding means lingering over its call, staying with the sound again and again. The fern on line 5 belongs to the pheasant, not the pigeon.

Lines 2 and 3 fill the kitchen with 'plumcakes', 'jellies' and 'gravy'. On line 4 Tom and Maggie keep going 'into the kitchen'. Line 5 says they stay away only when 'allowed to carry away' something. Line 6 calls it a 'load of booty', and line 7 shows them eating jam-puffs. So the booty is the food they were allowed to take from the kitchen.

Read line 43, where Maggie eats her puff with 'relish as well as rapidity'. The words 'as well as' join two separate things about how she ate. Rapidity means speed, so relish must be the other thing. Lines 45 and 46 show her lost in 'a vague sense of jam'. So relish is the enjoyment she took in the taste, not a sauce.
